newsitem.title: INDIA: Calcutta destitutes welcome Mother Teresa home.
newsitem.headline: Calcutta destitutes welcome Mother Teresa home.

text.p: Mother Teresa rested on Saturday during her first full day out of hospital as destitutes to whom she has devoted most of her life welcomed her return.
"We all prayed for the Mother and she has returned home. She will visit us after her full recovery," said an aged destitute at Calcutta's Nirmal Hriday (Immaculate Heart) hospice.
Mother Teresa, 86, a Nobel Peace laureate and Roman Catholic nun, left hospital at her own request on Friday after an 18-day battle against heart problems, malaria and pneumonia.
Sisters at Mother Teresa's Calcutta-based Missionaries of Charity religious order said she remained weak, had an irregular heartbeat and had been advised by doctors to take complete rest.
"Mother is very eager to return to her normal work. But she is still very weak and taking rest as per the advice of the doctors," Sister Priscilla, the Charity's spokeswoman, said.
"She is very happy to return home. She had a good sleep last night and she did not have any problems. Apart from some cardiac irregularity... she is alright," the sister said.
Mother Teresa's return to her home at the Charity's Mother House headquarters was also received with joy at other homes she set up for the deprived and the dying.
Sisters and volunteers at Nirmal Hriday and other homes, such as the Prem Dan (Gift of Love) and Shanti Dan (Gift of Peace), were jubiliant.
They held round-the-clock prayers when Mother Teresa, fitted with a cardiac pacemaker in 1989, was in Calcutta's Woodlands Nursing Home.
She was on an artificial respirator for much of the time in hospital from August 20.
"We prayed to God to take our lives and give it to Mother. She is our Mother and she has done so much for us," a 60-year- old patient with malnutrition told Reuters at Nirmal Hriday.
"I would have died a beast's death in one of the pavements of Calcutta. But, thanks to her, I am here and waiting for a peaceful death.
"My days are over and I pray for her. She has saved many destitutes like me. I know God will listen to our prayer and she will be alright," he added.
At Shanti Dan, for the mentally disabled, Teresa Singha said: "We know mother has returned to her house from hospital. We are eager to meet her. We know she will come to visit us."
Singha, who once tried to commit suicide, added: "I know I committed a sin. Now I find peace in prayer. I have been praying for Mother and God has listened to us."

The Missionaries of Charity, which she founded in 1949, runs some 544 homes for unwanted children and the destitute in more than 80 cities. The work includes the care of nearly 7,000 children in 120 homes and arranging 1,500 adoptions each year.
In 1991, Mother Teresa was treated at a Californian hospital for heart disease and bacterial pneumonia.
Two years later, she fell in Rome and broke three ribs. In August 1993, she developed malaria, complicated by her heart and lung problems. Last April, she fractured her left collar bone.
